name: Ipswich
title: Ipswich Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging | Grain and Bulk Ships
description: Thickness measurement at the Port of Ipswich for grain carriers, coasters and short-sea bulk ships: hold frames, hatch covers, tank tops and ballast tanks.
h1: Hold and Hull Thickness Measurement for Bulk Ships at the Port of Ipswich
intro: Ipswich is a river port at the head of the Orwell estuary, and its quays have shipped East Anglian grain for generations. The ships are coasters and short-sea bulk carriers that load grain after the harvest and bring in aggregates, feed and other dry bulks for the rest of the year. Before a grain cargo the holds must be clean and sound, which makes the loading call a natural moment to gauge. Technicians fly to the UK from India for each job and work the ship at her river berth.

highlights.p: Grain exports gather pace once the East Anglian harvest is in, and loading calls follow one another through the autumn and winter. An owner planning hold gauging can line it up with a grain call that is already fixed, instead of finding a separate window.

A grain cargo needs holds that are clean, dry and free of loose scale. Gauging frames, brackets and hold plating before loading also shows whether the wastage hiding behind flaking paint is cosmetic or structural, which is the question a renewal survey will ask.

The working berths are on the open river, tidal and close to the town centre. Ships stay alongside long enough to load or discharge a complete cargo, so most calls leave the team a useful working day once the scope has been agreed with the chief officer.

port.h: Ipswich: the Orwell's river port and its bulk trades
p: Ships bound for Ipswich enter the Orwell from Harwich Haven, past the container berths at Felixstowe, and follow a dredged channel several miles up a winding estuary to the town. They take a pilot for the passage, and because the channel and the berths are tidal, arrivals and departures are timed against the tide. On the way they pass beneath the Orwell Bridge, which carries the A14 high above the water and sets an air-draught limit for anything going upriver. At the head of the estuary the historic Wet Dock, entered through a lock, is now given over mostly to marinas and waterfront buildings; the commercial berths are on the river itself, at the quays and terminals along both banks below the dock.

Associated British Ports runs the port, which has long ranked among Britain's leading grain export ports. Wheat and barley from Suffolk, Essex and the wider region reach the quays by road and are loaded into short-sea ships for buyers on the Continent and further afield. Inbound trades are broader: marine-dredged and quarried aggregates for the construction industry, animal feed, fertiliser and other dry bulks, with some general cargo. The ships are mostly coasters and small to medium bulk carriers, many of them owned in northern Europe, with the occasional larger bulk carrier loading grain for a longer voyage. Many return to the Orwell several times a season on the same trade.

The calendar matters more here than at most ports. The harvest starts in high summer, and the export campaign builds through autumn and winter as merchants sell the crop, so grain ships are most frequent from late summer through the winter months. Each of those ships has to present clean holds, and one that fails a hold inspection loses time while the holds are washed and dried again. Inbound bulks keep the berths working outside the grain season. For gauging, the practical point is that a grain loading call brings the ship in with her holds empty, cleaned and about to be inspected, which is exactly the state the team needs for hold frame, bulkhead and tank-top readings.

facilities.h: Where gauging fits in at Ipswich
p: There is no ship-repair dry dock at Ipswich, so the work is done afloat at the river berths. Grain berths give the best chance for hold gauging, because the holds arrive empty and are cleaned and passed before loading begins; the team can work in each hold between the ship's arrival and the first grain going in, or in holds that the loading plan leaves until last. Aggregate and feed berths offer the reverse sequence, with holds becoming free as discharge progresses, and tank tops there are sometimes scored by grab work, which is worth recording when the readings are taken.

Ballast tanks and double-bottom tanks are more awkward on a loading call, because the ship deballasts as she loads and the chief officer needs the tanks in use. They are better gauged on a discharge call or during a wait for cargo, when one tank at a time can be emptied, ventilated and entered under the ship's permit system. Deck structure, hatch covers and coamings can be worked on almost any call. For docking, ships on these trades go to yards elsewhere in Britain or across the North Sea, and an Ipswich call a few weeks earlier is a good time to collect the steel quantities for the specification.
list: Grain export berths: hold frame, bracket, bulkhead and hold plating gauging after hold cleaning and before loading.
Aggregate discharge berths: tank-top thickness and grab damage records as each hold empties.
Dry bulk berths for feed and other cargoes: hatch cover, coaming and deck gauging while cargo is worked.
River berths during waits for cargo: ballast and double-bottom tank gauging under the ship's enclosed-space permit.
Larger bulk carriers loading grain for longer voyages: full hold surveys alongside the shipper's cargo-readiness checks.

context.h: Grain trade standards, port state control and European climate rules
p: Ships loading grain at Ipswich must meet the International Grain Code for stability, and charter parties normally require holds that are clean, dry, free of odour and free of loose rust scale before loading starts. Surveyors acting for the shippers inspect the holds and can reject them. Heavy scale on frames and brackets is a common reason for a failed hold inspection, and the same scale often hides wastage that a class surveyor would want gauged. Readings taken while the holds are open and clean answer both questions at once and save the owner a second look later.

Port state control at Ipswich is carried out by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency; the UK left the EU but stayed in the Paris MoU, which it now applies under domestic regulations. Older short-sea bulk carriers draw inspectors' attention to hatch covers, air pipes and ventilators because they decide weathertightness, and recent readings on those items are useful evidence when questions are asked. Grain voyages to EU ports also bring the larger ships into European climate rules: ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above fall under the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime for those voyages, while many smaller coasters sit below that threshold.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs at Ipswich
jobs.p: Ipswich jobs are mostly bulk-carrier work, and much of it is timed around grain. Managers ask for hold gauging on a loading call, when the holds are already clean, or for a pre-docking estimate on a ship that will dock in a few weeks' time. Pre-purchase work comes up when a short-sea bulk carrier changes hands, because buyers in this sector often inspect the ship on her normal trade rather than in a yard. We agree the order of work with the chief officer, the shipper's surveyor and the stevedores, so that gauging never delays the start of loading.
list: Hold frame and bracket gauging on a short-sea bulk carrier before loading wheat, with readings tied to frame numbers for the next renewal survey.
Tank-top and lower hopper readings on a ship discharging aggregates, with grab damage noted alongside the wastage.
Hatch cover, coaming and air-pipe gauging on an older coaster after weathertightness concerns were raised at an earlier port.
Pre-purchase gauging of a bulk carrier lying at a river berth between grain cargoes, scoped by the buyer's superintendent.
Ballast tank gauging during a wait for cargo, using the ship's enclosed-space permit and gas measurements before entry.

logistics: Teams usually fly into London Stansted, the closest of the London airports, or Heathrow, and reach Ipswich by rail or road; the town is on the main line from London Liverpool Street. The technicians come from India and need UK visas, so we start the application as soon as a call looks likely and follow the ship's movements from then on. The port gates are controlled by ABP, and the ship's agent arranges passes against each technician's passport and sets boarding times, which at Ipswich depend on the tide and the loading plan.
vessels: Dry bulk ships carrying feed and fertiliser
Occasional larger bulk carriers on longer grain voyages

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged at Ipswich before grain loading starts?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the best moment. The holds are empty, swept and washed, and the shipper's surveyor is about to inspect them, so frames, brackets, bulkheads and tank tops are as accessible as they will be outside a dry dock. We start as soon as the ship is alongside and the holds are released, finish each hold before loading reaches it, and work with the stevedores so the first grain goes in on time.

faqs.q: Does gauging interfere with a hold cleanliness inspection?
faqs.a: It should not. Readings are taken on small cleaned spots, and any scale removed to reach bare steel is swept up before the hold is presented. Where the paint is sound and the gauge's through-paint mode has been checked on a coated reference, readings can be taken without removing it. We tell the chief officer which holds are finished so the cleanliness inspection can follow in sequence.

faqs.q: When is the busiest time for grain ships at Ipswich?
faqs.a: Grain exports follow the harvest and the selling season, so the berths are busiest with grain ships from late summer through the winter, with fewer grain calls in late spring and early summer before the new crop. Owners who want hold gauging on a grain call have the widest choice of dates in those months, while discharge calls for aggregates and feed continue throughout the year.

faqs.q: Can ballast tanks be gauged on an Ipswich call?
faqs.a: On some calls. During grain loading the ship is deballasting and her tanks are in use, so entry is rarely practical. On a discharge call or during a wait for cargo, a tank can be emptied, ventilated, tested and entered under the ship's permit system. We plan ballast tank work for those calls and keep hold and deck work for the loading calls, so each visit is used for what it suits.
